text: To fill the faculty, Harper used Rockefeller's money the way few presidents could.
He offered salaries no one else could match and went hunting.
The most famous raid was on Clark University, in Worcester, Massachusetts.
Harper came away with something like two-thirds of its faculty and half of its graduate students.
The president of Clark never forgave him.

When the first classes opened on October 1, 1892, the University of Chicago already had a faculty of around a hundred and twenty, eight of them former college presidents, and an enrollment of 594 men and women.
A university that had not existed three years earlier opened its doors fully formed.
One of Harper's early hires tells you what kind of place he was building.
He brought in Amos Alonzo Stagg to run physical culture and coach football, and he gave Stagg a salary of twenty-five hundred dollars and a tenured professorship.
A football coach, on the regular faculty, with tenure.
That was nearly unheard of, and it set a pattern other universities would follow for decades.
The campus itself was designed by a Chicago architect named Henry Ives Cobb.
Cobb laid out a plan of six connected quadrangles and designed eighteen of the early buildings, all in English Gothic Revival, all faced in gray Bedford limestone from Indiana.
The first building finished was Cobb Hall, ready for that opening day in 1892, and it held the classrooms and offices the young university needed all at once.

Because Cobb worked from a single master plan, the buildings that came after his, raised by other architects over the following decades, kept to the same gray limestone and the same Gothic line, so the campus reads as one piece even though it went up over many years.
